◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives; solving one recovers the function from its rate of change — how we model growth, cooling, motion, and circuits. Separable equations are the first and simplest family.

Separable ODE
An equation dy/dx = g(x)h(y) is separable: move all y's to one side and x's to the other, then integrate: ∫ dy/h(y) = ∫ g(x) dx.
WORKED EXAMPLE — solving a separable equation

Solve dy/dx = xy, y(0) = 2.

Separate: dy/y = x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x²/2 + C.

Exponentiate: y = A·e^(x²/2). Apply y(0)=2: 2 = A·e⁰ = A, so y = 2e^(x²/2).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Don't forget the constant of integration C — and apply the initial condition AFTER integrating to pin it down. One C, on one side, is enough.

📊 FIGURE — A slope field with one solution threaded through
The little segments show the slope y′ prescribed by the ODE at each point — a wind map for solutions. A solution curve simply surfs the field, tangent to every segment it passes. Sketching a few field segments often reveals the behavior before any algebra.
📊 FIGURE — getting each variable to its own side
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Solving dy/dx = (1 + y)/x for x > 0

Separate — the y-terms with dy, the x-terms with dx:

dy/(1 + y) = dx/x

Integrate both sides:

ln|1 + y| = ln|x| + C₁

Exponentiate. The constant e^{C₁} is just a new positive constant, and absorbing the sign lets it be any nonzero C:

1 + y = Cx  ⟹  y = Cx − 1

Check it: y′ = C, while (1 + y)/x = (1 + Cx − 1)/x = Cx/x = C. ✓

Similarly dy/dx = y² separates as y⁻² dy = dx, giving ∫dy/y² = ∫dx and then −1/y = x + C.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Separation means dividing until every y sits with dy and every x with dx, then integrating. Two habits save marks: exponentiate carefully — e^{ln|x| + C} becomes C·x, not x + C — and always verify by substituting your answer back into the original equation.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch1/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Many models aren't separable but ARE linear: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). The integrating factor is a systematic recipe that solves every equation of this form.

Integrating factor
For dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), the integrating factor is μ = e^{∫P dx}. Multiplying through makes the left side (μy)', so μy = ∫ μQ dx + C.
WORKED EXAMPLE — integrating factor method

Solve dy/dx + 2y = 6, y(0)=1.

P = 2, so μ = e^{∫2 dx} = e^{2x}. Multiply: (e^{2x}y)' = 6e^{2x}.

Integrate: e^{2x}y = 3e^{2x} + C ⇒ y = 3 + Ce^{-2x}. y(0)=1 ⇒ 1 = 3 + C ⇒ C = −2, so y = 3 − 2e^{-2x}.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Put the equation in STANDARD form (coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1) before reading off P(x). A leading coefficient must be divided out first.

📊 FIGURE — The integrating-factor pipeline
Multiply the standard form by μ = e^(∫P dx) and the left side collapses into one exact derivative — then integrating both sides is easy. The whole method is this one assembly line.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch1/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

First-order ODEs describe any process whose rate depends on the current state: population growth, radioactive decay, Newton's cooling, and mixing-tank problems — the workhorses of applied math.

Newton's Law of Cooling
dT/dt = −k(T − Tenv): the temperature changes at a rate proportional to the difference from the surroundings. Solution: T = Tenv + (T₀ − Tenv)e^{-kt}.
WORKED EXAMPLE — mixing tank

A tank holds 100 L of water. Brine (2 g/L) flows in at 5 L/min; the well-mixed solution drains at 5 L/min. Set up the ODE for salt A(t).

Rate in = (2 g/L)(5 L/min) = 10 g/min. Rate out = (A/100 g/L)(5 L/min) = A/20 g/min.

dA/dt = 10 − A/20 — a linear first-order ODE. Equilibrium (dA/dt = 0): A = 200 g.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

In mixing problems the OUTFLOW concentration is (current amount)/(current volume), which changes over time — don't treat it as constant unless volume is constant.

📊 FIGURE — Logistic growth: exponential start, capped finish
Small populations grow almost exponentially (bottom left), but the (1 − P/K) brake strengthens as P nears the carrying capacity K, bending the curve into an S that levels off. The inflection — fastest growth — happens exactly at P = K/2.
📊 FIGURE — decay by repeated halving
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Fraction remaining after 15 years with a 5-year half-life

Fifteen years is 15/5 = 3 half-lives, so the amount halves three times:

(1/2)³ = 1/8 = 0.125

The exponential route agrees: k = ln 2 / 5 = 0.13863, and e^{−0.13863 × 15} = e^{−2.0794} = 0.125.

Counting half-lives is faster whenever the elapsed time is a whole multiple of T — reach for the exponential formula only when it is not.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Count half-lives before reaching for the formula. Elapsed time divided by the half-life gives n, and the fraction remaining is (1/2)ⁿ — here 15/5 = 3, so 1/8. Use k = ln 2 / T with A₀e^{−kt} only when the elapsed time is not a whole multiple.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch2/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Second-order linear ODEs ay'' + by' + cy = 0 model vibration, circuits, and control systems. Their solutions are found from a simple algebra step: the characteristic equation.

Characteristic equation
For ay'' + by' + cy = 0, substitute y = e^{rt} to get ar² + br + c = 0. The roots r determine the solution form.
Solution by root type
Distinct real r₁,r₂: y = c₁e^{r₁t} + c₂e^{r₂t}. Repeated root r: y = (c₁ + c₂t)e^{rt}. Complex r = α ± βi: y = e^{αt}(c₁cos βt + c₂sin βt).
WORKED EXAMPLE — distinct real roots

Solve y'' − 5y' + 6y = 0.

Characteristic: r² − 5r + 6 = 0 ⇒ (r−2)(r−3) = 0 ⇒ r = 2, 3.

General solution: y = c₁e^{2t} + c₂e^{3t}.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A REPEATED root gives an extra factor of t (that's why the second solution is te^{rt}) — you can't just write c₁e^{rt} + c₂e^{rt}, which is really one solution.

📊 FIGURE — The three faces of the characteristic roots
Two distinct real roots: a mix of pure exponentials. A repeated root: the xe^(rx) factor bends the curve. Complex roots α ± βi: oscillation inside an exponential envelope. Reading the discriminant of r² + br + c tells you which picture you are in.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch2/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real systems have a driving force: ay'' + by' + cy = f(t). The full solution is y = yh (homogeneous) + yp (particular). Undetermined coefficients guesses yp from the shape of f(t).

Guessing y_p
For f(t) polynomial → try a polynomial; f = e^{kt} → try Ae^{kt}; f = cos/sin(ωt) → try A cos ωt + B sin ωt. If your guess already solves the homogeneous equation, multiply it by t.
WORKED EXAMPLE — particular solution

Find y_p for y'' − y = 3e^{2t}.

Guess y_p = Ae^{2t}. Then y_p'' = 4Ae^{2t}, so 4Ae^{2t} − Ae^{2t} = 3Ae^{2t} = 3e^{2t}.

So 3A = 3 ⇒ A = 1, giving y_p = e^{2t}. Full solution: y = c₁e^{t} + c₂e^{-t} + e^{2t}.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

If your trial y_p is already a homogeneous solution (resonance), it collapses to 0 — multiply the guess by t (or t²) until it's independent.

📊 FIGURE — Undetermined coefficients: the guess catalog
The trial solution copies the forcing’s family with unknown coefficients; plug in and solve for them. If the guess collides with a homogeneous solution, multiply by x. Mixed forcings sum their guesses.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch2/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The equation mx'' + cx' + kx = F(t) is THE model of a vibrating system — springs, buildings, circuits. The damping term c and forcing F determine whether it oscillates, decays, or blows up in resonance.

Damping cases
Undamped (c=0): pure oscillation. Underdamped: decaying oscillation. Critically damped: fastest non-oscillating return. Overdamped: slow non-oscillating return. Set by the discriminant c² − 4mk.
WORKED EXAMPLE — classifying a system

For x'' + 4x' + 3x = 0 (m=1, c=4, k=3): characteristic r² + 4r + 3 = 0 ⇒ (r+1)(r+3) ⇒ r = −1, −3.

Two distinct negative real roots ⇒ OVERDAMPED: it returns to rest without oscillating.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency ω₀ = √(k/m) in an UNDAMPED system — the amplitude grows without bound. Damping prevents unbounded growth.

📊 FIGURE — Underdamped oscillation inside its decaying envelope
The solution e^(−ct)·cos(ωt) rings at the natural frequency while the exponential envelope (dashed) throttles the amplitude down. More damping squeezes the envelope faster; at critical damping the oscillation disappears entirely.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch3/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Laplace transform turns a differential equation into an ALGEBRA problem: derivatives become multiplication by s. It's the engineer's favorite tool for IVPs, especially with switches and impulses.

Laplace transform
ℒ{f(t)} = F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^{-st}f(t) dt. Key pairs: ℒ{1} = 1/s, ℒ{e^{at}} = 1/(s−a), ℒ{t} = 1/s², ℒ{cos ωt} = s/(s²+ω²), ℒ{sin ωt} = ω/(s²+ω²).
Transform of derivatives
ℒ{y'} = sY − y(0); ℒ{y''} = s²Y − s·y(0) − y'(0). This is what converts the ODE to algebra AND builds in the initial conditions.
WORKED EXAMPLE — a simple transform

Find ℒ{3 + 2e^{4t}}.

By linearity: 3·ℒ{1} + 2·ℒ{e^{4t}} = 3/s + 2/(s−4).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The transform of a derivative carries the initial conditions with it (the −y(0) terms). That's a feature — it bakes the IVP into the algebra, so you never separately solve for the constants.

📊 FIGURE — The Laplace transform is a bridge
Hard calculus (a differential equation in t) crosses into easy algebra (a rational equation in s), gets solved by rearranging and partial fractions, then crosses back via the inverse transform. All the difficulty concentrates in the final inversion — hence the tables.
📊 FIGURE — the transforms worth knowing cold
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — ℒ{1} straight from the integral

Apply the definition with f(t) = 1:

ℒ{1} = ∫₀^∞ e^{−st}·1 dt = [−e^{−st}/s]₀^∞

For s > 0 the term e^{−st} → 0 as t → ∞, so the upper limit contributes 0, and the lower limit contributes −(−1/s):

ℒ{1} = 0 − (−1/s) = 1/s

The condition s > 0 is not decoration — for s ≤ 0 the integral diverges. Every Laplace transform carries such a region of convergence, even when tables omit it.

🎯 EXAM TIP
ℒ{1} = 1/s. Build the small table outward from the definition — 1 ↦ 1/s, t ↦ 1/s², e^{at} ↦ 1/(s − a) — and note the pattern that multiplying by t raises the power of s by one.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch3/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

This is the payoff: transform both sides, solve the resulting algebraic equation for Y(s), then invert. Initial conditions are handled automatically.

The method
(1) Take ℒ of the whole ODE, using the derivative rules with the given y(0), y'(0). (2) Solve algebraically for Y(s). (3) Use partial fractions + the table to find y(t) = ℒ⁻¹{Y(s)}.
WORKED EXAMPLE — solving an IVP

Solve y' + y = 0, y(0) = 4.

Transform: sY − 4 + Y = 0 ⇒ (s+1)Y = 4 ⇒ Y = 4/(s+1).

Invert: y(t) = 4e^{-t}. (Matches the separable answer.)

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Always substitute the numeric initial values (y(0), y'(0)) into the derivative transforms immediately — leaving them symbolic is where errors creep in.

📊 FIGURE — The Laplace transform is a bridge
Hard calculus (a differential equation in t) crosses into easy algebra (a rational equation in s), gets solved by rearranging and partial fractions, then crosses back via the inverse transform. All the difficulty concentrates in the final inversion — hence the tables.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch3/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Laplace's superpower is handling forces that switch on/off or spike — a voltage applied at t=2, an impulse hammer-blow. The unit step function and the Dirac delta make these tractable where other methods struggle.

Unit step function
u(t−a) = 0 for t < a, 1 for t ≥ a (a switch turning on at t = a). ℒ{u(t−a)} = e^{-as}/s.
Second shifting theorem
ℒ{u(t−a)f(t−a)} = e^{-as}F(s). The e^{-as} factor in an s-domain expression signals a time delay of a.
WORKED EXAMPLE — transform with a step

A force turns on at t = 3: f(t) = u(t−3). Its transform is ℒ{u(t−3)} = e^{-3s}/s.

Seeing e^{-as} in Y(s) tells you the response is time-shifted: the effect appears starting at t = a.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The exponential factor e^{-as} in the s-domain always means a TIME SHIFT by a in the t-domain — not exponential growth. Recognizing it is key to inverting.

📊 FIGURE — The unit step: forcing that switches on
u(t − a) is 0, then snaps to 1 at t = a — the mathematical light switch. Multiply by it to turn any forcing on (or off) at a chosen moment; in the s-domain that adds a factor e^(−as). The impulse δ(t − a) is its idealized instantaneous cousin.
📊 FIGURE — what e^{−as} does
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Inverting e^{−πs}/(s² + 1)

First invert without the exponential factor: ℒ⁻¹{1/(s² + 1)} = sin t.

The factor e^{−πs} delays that result by π and switches it on at t = π:

u(t − π) sin(t − π)

Then simplify using sin(t − π) = −sin t:

= −u(t − π) sin t

So the response is zero until t = π and equals −sin t thereafter. Both forms are correct; the second is tidier and is what a multiple-choice option will usually show.

🎯 EXAM TIP
A factor of e^{−as} in the s-domain means a delay of a in the t-domain, with a unit step switching the function on. Do the inversion first and apply the shift second — and remember the trig identity that follows, since sin(t − π) = −sin t is what turns the answer into the simpler form.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch4/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Coupled quantities (predator–prey, coupled tanks, multi-loop circuits) form a SYSTEM x' = Ax. The solution comes straight from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A — a beautiful link back to linear algebra.

Eigenvalue solution
For x' = Ax, each eigenpair (λ, v) gives a solution x = ve^{λt}. The general solution is a combination: x = c₁v₁e^{λ₁t} + c₂v₂e^{λ₂t}.
WORKED EXAMPLE — solving a system

For x' = Ax with eigenvalues λ = 1, −2 and eigenvectors v₁, v₂:

x(t) = c₁v₁e^{t} + c₂v₂e^{-2t}. The e^{t} term grows; the e^{-2t} term decays — so trajectories are pushed along v₁.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Signs of the eigenvalues tell the whole story: all negative → stable (decays to 0); any positive → unstable; complex → spirals/oscillation.

📊 FIGURE — Phase portraits: the eigenvalues choose the picture
Both eigenvalues negative: a sink — everything spirals home along the eigen-directions. Opposite signs: a saddle — in along one axis, flung out along the other. Complex eigenvalues: spirals (decaying if the real part is negative). Eigen-analysis IS the qualitative theory.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch4/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most ODEs have NO closed-form solution. Numerical methods like Euler's approximate the solution step by step — the foundation of every physics engine and simulation.

Euler's method
To solve y' = f(t,y), y(t₀)=y₀: step with yn+1 = yn + h·f(tn, yn), where h is the step size. Follow the slope field one small step at a time.
WORKED EXAMPLE — one Euler step

For y' = y, y(0) = 1, with h = 0.1, take one step.

y₁ = y₀ + h·f(t₀,y₀) = 1 + 0.1·(1) = 1.1.

The exact value is e^{0.1} ≈ 1.105 — Euler undershoots slightly; smaller h reduces the error.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Euler's method has error proportional to the step size h: halving h roughly halves the error but doubles the work. Fancier methods (Runge–Kutta) get far more accuracy per step.

📊 FIGURE — Euler’s method: chasing a curve with straight steps
Start on the true solution (green) and repeatedly step along the CURRENT tangent slope for a width h. The polyline drifts from the curve — error builds each step — but shrinking h (or upgrading to RK4’s four slope samples) tightens the chase dramatically.
"}, "DIFFEQ/ch4/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before solving, it's worth knowing whether a solution EXISTS and is UNIQUE, and what it does qualitatively — sometimes the phase line tells you everything without a formula.

Existence–uniqueness
If f(t,y) and ∂f/∂y are continuous near (t₀,y₀), the IVP y'=f(t,y), y(t₀)=y₀ has a unique solution nearby. Continuity guarantees existence; a bounded ∂f/∂y guarantees uniqueness.
Equilibria
Constant solutions where y' = 0. An equilibrium is STABLE if nearby solutions approach it, UNSTABLE if they move away — read off from the sign of f around it.
WORKED EXAMPLE — phase line analysis

For y' = y(1−y) (logistic), equilibria are y = 0 and y = 1.

For 00 (increasing); for y>1, y'<0 (decreasing). So y=1 is STABLE (carrying capacity) and y=0 is UNSTABLE.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

An equilibrium's stability is determined by the SIGN of y' on each side, not by the equilibrium value itself. Sketch the phase line to classify without solving.

📊 FIGURE — A slope field with one solution threaded through
The little segments show the slope y′ prescribed by the ODE at each point — a wind map for solutions. A solution curve simply surfs the field, tangent to every segment it passes. Sketching a few field segments often reveals the behavior before any algebra.
📊 FIGURE — checking the hypotheses
🎯 EXAM TIP
For y′ = t/(y − 2) the theorem gives no guarantee near y = 2, where f is undefined and discontinuous. Read the conclusion precisely: failing the hypotheses means the theorem is silent, not that a solution fails to exist. It also guarantees only a local solution — an interval around t₀, not all t.
"}, "DIFFEQ/solving/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

A separable equation has the form dy/dx = g(x)h(y). Rewrite as dy/h(y) = g(x) dx and integrate both sides, then apply the initial condition to find the constant.

Linear first-order

For y' + P(x)y = Q(x), compute the integrating factor μ = e^(∫P(x) dx). Multiply through so the left side becomes (μy)', then integrate: μy = ∫μQ dx + C, and y = (1/μ)(∫μQ dx + C).

Exponential models

Growth/decay obey dP/dt = kP, whose solution is P(t) = P₀e^(kt). For decay k < 0; the half-life T satisfies (1/2) = e^(kT), so after n half-lives a fraction (1/2)ⁿ remains.

Worked example

Solve y' + 2y = 0, y(0) = 4. Here μ = e^(∫2 dx) = e^(2x). Then (e^(2x)y)' = 0, so e^(2x)y = C and y = Ce^(-2x). Applying y(0) = 4 gives C = 4, so y = 4e^(-2x).

Always substitute your solution back into the original equation and the initial condition to verify before choosing an answer.

"}, "DIFFEQ/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

For a constant-coefficient equation ay'' + by' + cy = 0, substitute y = e^(rx) to get the characteristic equation ar² + br + c = 0. The roots determine the general solution:

  • Real distinct r₁ ≠ r₂: y = c₁e^(r₁x) + c₂e^(r₂x)
  • Repeated r: y = (c₁ + c₂x)e^(rx)
  • Complex r = α ± βi: y = e^(αx)(c₁cos βx + c₂sin βx)

Undetermined coefficients

For ay'' + by' + cy = f(x), guess a particular solution y_p matching the form of f: a constant for a constant f, Ae^(kx) for an exponential, etc. Substitute and solve for the coefficient.

Classifying equilibria

For x' = Ax, find the eigenvalues of A. Real eigenvalues of the same sign give a node (stable if negative), opposite signs give a saddle, and pure imaginary eigenvalues give a center.

Worked example

Solve y'' + 4y = 0. The characteristic equation r² + 4 = 0 gives r = ±2i, so y = c₁cos 2x + c₂sin 2x.

"}, "DIFFEQ/solving_only/sim": {"body": "

🧮 Solving Only

A practice set of only computational problems pulled from across this whole course — work out the answer and pick it from the options. Concept and definition questions are filtered out, so every item is something to solve. Reshuffled each time you start.

"}, "DIFFEQ/solving2/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

A separable equation dy/dx = g(x)h(y) is solved by writing dy/h(y) = g(x) dx and integrating both sides, then applying the initial condition to fix the constant.

A linear first-order equation has the form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). Compute the integrating factor μ = e^(∫P dx). Multiplying through gives (μy)' = μQ, so μy = ∫μQ dx + C and y = (1/μ)(∫μQ dx + C).

Worked mini-example

Solve dy/dx + y = 2, y(0) = 5. Here P = 1, so μ = e^x. Then (e^x y)' = 2e^x, giving e^x y = 2e^x + C, so y = 2 + Ce^(-x). The condition y(0) = 5 gives 5 = 2 + C, so C = 3 and y = 2 + 3e^(-x). As x → ∞ the transient dies and y → 2.

Growth and decay

Exponential models obey P = P₀ e^(kt). With a doubling time T, after n = t/T doublings P = P₀ · 2ⁿ. With a half-life H, after n = t/H half-lives P = P₀ / 2ⁿ. Count whole periods when they divide evenly.

"}, "DIFFEQ/solving2/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

For a constant-coefficient equation ay'' + by' + cy = 0, substitute y = e^(rx) to get the characteristic equation ar² + br + c = 0. Solve for r using the quadratic formula.

General-solution forms

  • Distinct real roots r₁, r₂: y = c₁e^(r₁x) + c₂e^(r₂x).
  • Repeated root r: y = (c₁ + c₂x)e^(rx).
  • Complex roots α ± βi: y = e^(αx)(c₁cos βx + c₂sin βx).

Undetermined coefficients

For ay'' + by' + cy = f(x), guess a particular solution y_p shaped like f: a constant for a constant, Ax + B for a linear f, and so on. Substitute and match coefficients.

Worked mini-example

Solve y'' + y = 2x. Guess y_p = Ax + B, so y_p'' = 0 and 0 + Ax + B = 2x gives A = 2, B = 0, hence y_p = 2x.

Classifying 2D linear systems

For x' = Ax, examine the eigenvalues of A: two positive reals give an unstable node (source), two negative reals a stable node (sink), opposite signs a saddle, and pure imaginary a center.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
THE 3-STEP LOOP
\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
\n
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
\n\n\n\n\n
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.

"}, "DIFFEQ/cheat/c2": {"body": "

📋 Second-Order Linear ODEs

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Homogeneous Equations & the Characteristic Root

▸ Characteristic equation For ay'' + by' + cy = 0, substitute y = e^{rt} to get ar² + br + c = 0. The roots r determine the solution form.

📋 Laplace Transforms

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

The Laplace Transform & Its Inverse

▸ Laplace transform ℒ{f(t)} = F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^{-st}f(t) dt. Key pairs: ℒ{1} = 1/s, ℒ{e^{at}} = 1/(s−a), ℒ{t} = 1/s², ℒ{cos ωt} = s/(s²+ω²), ℒ{sin ωt} = ω/(s²+ω²).

▸ Transform of derivatives ℒ{y'} = sY − y(0); ℒ{y''} = s²Y − s·y(0) − y'(0). This is what converts the ODE to algebra AND builds in the initial conditions.

Solving IVPs with Laplace Transforms

▸ The method (1) Take ℒ of the whole ODE, using the derivative rules with the given y(0), y'(0). (2) Solve algebraically for Y(s). (3) Use partial fractions + the table to find y(t) = ℒ⁻¹{Y(s)}.

Step Functions & Discontinuous Forcing

▸ Second shifting theorem ℒ{u(t−a)f(t−a)} = e^{-as}F(s). The e^{-as} factor in an s-domain expression signals a time delay of a.

Systems of Linear ODEs & the Eigenvalue Method

▸ Eigenvalue solution For x' = Ax, each eigenpair (λ, v) gives a solution x = ve^{λt}. The general solution is a combination: x = c₁v₁e^{λ₁t} + c₂v₂e^{λ₂t}.

Euler's Method & Numerical Solutions

▸ Euler's method To solve y' = f(t,y), y(t₀)=y₀: step with y n+1 = y n + h·f(t n , y n ), where h is the step size. Follow the slope field one small step at a time.

Existence, Uniqueness & Qualitative Behavior

▸ Existence–uniqueness If f(t,y) and ∂f/∂y are continuous near (t₀,y₀), the IVP y'=f(t,y), y(t₀)=y₀ has a unique solution nearby. Continuity guarantees existence; a bounded ∂f/∂y guarantees uniqueness.
